title: Run-length encoding
spec:
Write a Python function `rle_encode(s: str) -> str` that run-length encodes a string.
Each maximal run of the same character becomes the character followed by the run length in decimal
(the count is ALWAYS written, even when it is 1). The input never contains digit characters.
Examples: rle_encode("aaabcc") == "a3b1c2", rle_encode("") == "".
Characters are compared exactly (case-sensitive; spaces and punctuation are ordinary characters).

title: Bracket balance check
spec:
Write a Python function `is_balanced(s: str) -> bool` that returns True iff the brackets
(), [] and {} in `s` are balanced and properly nested. All other characters are ignored.
The empty string is balanced.

title: Roman numeral to int
spec:
Write a Python function `roman_to_int(s: str) -> int` converting a valid Roman numeral
(standard subtractive notation, values 1..3999, uppercase letters IVXLCDM) to an integer.

title: Top-k frequent words
spec:
Write a Python function `top_k_words(text: str, k: int) -> list[tuple[str, int]]`.
A word is a maximal run of ASCII letters a-z or A-Z; every other character (digits, apostrophes,
hyphens, spaces, non-ASCII letters, ...) is a separator. Words are compared case-insensitively and
reported in lowercase. Return the k most frequent words as (word, count) tuples, sorted by count
descending, then word ascending. If there are fewer than k distinct words, return all of them.
k >= 0.

title: Fix buggy lower-bound binary search
spec:
The following function is supposed to return the smallest index i such that arr[i] >= x,
or len(arr) if no such index exists. `arr` is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain
duplicates or be empty. It must run in O(log n). The implementation is buggy (wrong results and it can
loop forever). Fix it and return the complete corrected function.

```python
def first_ge(arr, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if arr[mid] < x:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return lo
```

title: Merge intervals
spec:
Write a Python function `merge_intervals(intervals: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]`.
Each interval is [start, end] with start <= end (closed interval). Merge all overlapping intervals;
intervals that merely touch (e.g. [1,2] and [2,3]) also merge. Return the merged intervals sorted by
start. The input may be unsorted and empty. Do not modify the input list or its inner lists.

title: LRU cache class
spec:
Implement a Python class `LRUCache` with:
- `__init__(self, capacity: int)` (capacity >= 1)
- `get(self, key) -> value`: return the stored value, or -1 if absent. A successful get marks the key
  as most recently used.
- `put(self, key, value) -> None`: insert or update. Updating an existing key also marks it most
  recently used. If inserting a new key exceeds capacity, evict the least recently used key first.
Both operations must be O(1) average.

title: Coin change: number of ways
spec:
Write a Python function `coin_change_ways(amount: int, coins: list[int]) -> int` returning the
number of distinct combinations (order does not matter) of coins that sum to `amount`, using each coin
denomination unlimited times, modulo 1_000_000_007. `coins` holds distinct positive integers and may be
empty. amount >= 0; the number of ways to make 0 is 1.

title: Grid shortest path (BFS)
spec:
Write a Python function `shortest_path(grid: list[str]) -> int`. The grid rows are equal-length
strings made of '.', '#', 'S', 'E' (exactly one 'S' and exactly one 'E'). From 'S', move one cell up,
down, left or right per step; '#' is a wall and you may not leave the grid. Return the minimum number
of steps to reach 'E', or -1 if unreachable.

title: Topological order with cycle detection
spec:
Write a Python function `topo_order(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[int] | None`.
Nodes are 0..n-1; an edge (u, v) means u must come before v. Return the lexicographically smallest
topological ordering (as a list of all n nodes), or None if the graph has a cycle (including a
self-loop). Duplicate edges may appear. n >= 0.

title: Largest all-ones rectangle
spec:
Write a Python function `max_rectangle(matrix: list[str]) -> int` returning the area of the largest
axis-aligned rectangle containing only '1' characters. Rows are equal-length strings of '0'/'1'.
The matrix may be empty ([]), and rows may be empty strings. Must handle 200x200 within a second.

title: Fix buggy nested-list flatten
spec:
The following function should flatten arbitrarily nested lists and tuples into a single flat
list, preserving order. ONLY list and tuple objects are expanded; everything else (including str,
bytes, dict, set, None, numbers) is kept as a single element. Every call must be independent of
previous calls. It is buggy. Fix it and return the complete corrected function (same name and a
signature callable as flatten(nested)).

```python
def flatten(nested, out=[]):
    for item in nested:
        if hasattr(item, '__iter__'):
            flatten(item, out)
        else:
            out.append(item)
    return out
```

title: Fix buggy interval scheduling
spec:
The following function should return the maximum number of pairwise non-overlapping intervals.
Intervals are half-open [s, e) with s < e, so [1,2) and [2,3) do NOT overlap. The input is a list of
(s, e) tuples and must not be modified. It is buggy. Fix it and return the complete corrected function.

```python
def max_non_overlapping(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])
    count, end = 0, float('-inf')
    for s, e in intervals:
        if s > end:
            count += 1
            end = e
    return count
```

title: Integer expression evaluator (no eval/ast)
spec:
Write a Python function `evaluate(expr: str) -> int` that evaluates an integer arithmetic expression
WITHOUT using eval/exec/ast/compile. Grammar:
- non-negative integer literals (decimal digits only), binary + - * /, parentheses, unary + and -
  (unary operators may repeat, e.g. "--3" == 3), arbitrary spaces between tokens.
- * and / bind tighter than + and -; all binary operators are left-associative; unary binds tighter
  than binary operators.
- / is integer division truncating toward zero (e.g. -7/2 == -3, 7/-2 == -3).
- division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError.
- any malformed input (empty, unknown characters, missing operands, unbalanced parentheses,
  two adjacent numbers like "2 3") raises ValueError.

title: JSON parser (no json module)
spec:
Write a Python function `parse_json(s: str)` that parses a JSON text per RFC 8259 WITHOUT using the
json module, eval, or ast. Return Python values: object->dict, array->list, string->str,
integer->int, number with fraction or exponent->float, true/false/null->True/False/None.
Support whitespace (space, tab, CR, LF) around tokens, string escapes \" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t and \uXXXX
(surrogate pairs need not be combined). Be strict: raise ValueError for any invalid input, including
trailing commas, single quotes, leading zeros like 01, unescaped control characters in strings,
trailing garbage after the value, and empty input.

title: Bank transaction simulator
spec:
Write a Python function `simulate_bank(customers: list[tuple[int, int]], tellers: int) -> list[tuple[int, int, int]]`.
Discrete-event simulation of a bank with `tellers` tellers (indexed 0..tellers-1, tellers >= 1) and a
single FIFO queue. customers[i] = (arrival_time, service_time), integers >= 0, NOT necessarily sorted.
Customers join the queue in order of arrival time; ties are broken by their index in the input list.
The customer at the front of the queue starts service at the earliest moment t >= its arrival time at
which any teller is free (a teller that finishes at time t is free at time t); it goes to the
LOWEST-INDEXED teller free at t. Service occupies the teller during [start, start+service_time).
A service time of 0 is allowed (the teller is immediately free again at the same time).
Return, in the ORIGINAL input order, a list of (teller_index, start_time, end_time) per customer.

title: Cheapest flight within k stops
spec:
Write a Python function `cheapest_price(n: int, flights: list[tuple[int, int, int]], src: int, dst: int, k: int) -> int`.
Cities are 0..n-1; flights[i] = (u, v, price) is a directed flight with price >= 0 (there may be
several flights between the same pair). Return the cheapest total price from src to dst using at most
k intermediate stops (i.e. at most k+1 flights), or -1 if impossible. If src == dst the answer is 0.
Must handle n=200, 5000 flights, k=50 quickly.

title: Minimum window substring
spec:
Write a Python function `min_window(s: str, t: str) -> str` returning the shortest contiguous substring of
`s` that contains every character of `t` with at least the same multiplicity (case-sensitive).
If several shortest windows exist, return the leftmost one. If none exists, or t is empty, return "".
Must be O(len(s) + len(t)) or close to it (len(s) up to 200_000).

title: Edit distance with operation script
spec:
Write a Python function `edit_distance_ops(a: str, b: str) -> tuple[int, list[str]]` returning the
Levenshtein distance between a and b (insert, delete, substitute each cost 1) together with ONE optimal
edit script that transforms a into b. The script is a list of operations applied left to right to a
working string that starts equal to a, where each op is one of:
  "I{i}{c}"  insert character c so that it ends up at index i   (e.g. "I0x")
  "D{i}"     delete the character at index i                    (e.g. "D3")
  "S{i}{c}"  replace the character at index i with c            (e.g. "S2z")
Indices refer to the working string at the moment the op is applied. Characters are single non-digit
characters. len(script) must equal the distance. Must handle strings of length 500 within a second.

title: Regex engine without re
spec:
Write a Python function `regex_fullmatch(pattern: str, s: str) -> bool` implementing a small regex engine
WITHOUT using the `re` module (or any regex library). Return True iff the WHOLE string s matches.
Syntax:
- Special characters are  . * + ? { } ( ) [ ] | \  . Any other character is a literal.
- `\c` (backslash + any character) is the literal c. A trailing lone backslash is an error.
- `.` matches any single character.
- Character class `[...]`: optional leading `^` for negation, then one or more items; an item is a single
  character (or `\c` escape) or a range `a-z` (range with lo > hi is an error). A `-` that is first or last in the
  class is literal. `]` must be escaped inside a class. Unterminated class is an error. Empty class `[]` is an error.
- Grouping `( ... )`; an empty group `()` matches the empty string.
- Alternation `|` has the lowest precedence; empty alternatives are allowed (`a|` matches "" or "a").
- Quantifiers `*`, `+`, `?`, `{m}`, `{m,}`, `{m,n}` (m, n decimal, m <= n) apply to the immediately preceding
  atom (literal, `.`, class, or group). A quantifier with nothing to apply to, a quantifier directly after
  another quantifier (e.g. `a**`, `a{2}?`), a malformed or unterminated `{...}`, or a bare `}` or `]` outside a
  class is an error. An unmatched `(` or `)` is an error.
- Errors raise ValueError (for any input s, including when the pattern is checked first).
- Matching must take polynomial time: e.g. pattern "(a*)*b" against "a"*40 must return False quickly.

title: POSIX-like shell tokenizer (no shlex)
spec:
Write a Python function `shell_split(s: str) -> list[str]` that splits a command line into words using
these POSIX-shell-like rules (do NOT use the shlex module):
- Unquoted whitespace (space, tab, newline) separates words; runs of whitespace count as one separator.
- Single quotes: every character up to the next single quote is literal (no escapes inside).
- Double quotes: characters are literal, except a backslash followed by one of  "  \  $  `  or newline: the
  backslash is removed and the next character kept literally — except backslash+newline inside double quotes,
  which removes BOTH characters (line continuation). A backslash before any other character is kept together
  with that character (both characters stay).
- Unquoted backslash: the backslash is removed and the next character is literal (e.g. `a\ b` is one word
  "a b"). Unquoted backslash+newline removes both characters and does NOT split the word.
- Quoted and unquoted parts that touch form one word: a'b'"c" -> "abc". A standalone '' or "" is an empty word.
- An unquoted # that appears where a new word would start begins a comment that runs up to (not including) the
  next newline; a # inside a word (a#b) or inside quotes is literal.
- Unterminated single/double quotes, or a backslash as the very last character outside single quotes, raise
  ValueError.

title: Assembly interpreter with pre-validation
spec:
Write a Python function `run_program(src: str) -> list[int]` that interprets a tiny assembly language and
returns the list of values written by `out`.
Syntax: one statement per line. `;` starts a comment to end of line. Blank lines are ignored. Tokens are
separated by whitespace (no commas). A line of the form `name:` (alone on its line) defines a label;
label names match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. Registers are single lowercase letters a-z, all initially 0.
An operand written `x` below is either a register or a signed decimal integer literal (e.g. -5); `r` must be a
register; `L` must be a label.
Instructions:
  mov r x | add r x | sub r x | mul r x
  div r x   r = r / x truncated toward zero          (x == 0 -> ZeroDivisionError)
  mod r x   r = r - x * trunc(r / x) (sign follows r) (x == 0 -> ZeroDivisionError)
  jmp L | jz x L (jump if x == 0) | jnz x L (jump if x != 0)
  call L    push the index of the next instruction on the call stack, jump to L
  ret       pop the call stack and jump there; if the call stack is empty, halt
  push x    push onto the value stack (separate from the call stack)
  pop r     pop the value stack into r (empty value stack -> IndexError)
  out x     append the value to the output
  halt
Execution starts at the first instruction and halts on `halt`, on `ret` with an empty call stack, or when
running past the last instruction. The whole program is validated BEFORE execution: unknown instruction,
wrong operand count, invalid register/operand, undefined label, or duplicate label raise ValueError even if
that line would never execute. If more than 1_000_000 instructions would be executed, raise RuntimeError.
Must execute ~500k instructions in well under 3 seconds.

title: Count distinct palindromic subsequences
spec:
Write a Python function `count_pal_subseq(s: str) -> int` returning the number of DISTINCT non-empty
palindromic subsequences of s (as strings), modulo 1_000_000_007. s consists of lowercase letters a-z,
0 <= len(s) <= 600. Must run in under 2 seconds for len(s) = 600.
Example: "bccb" -> 6 ("b", "c", "bb", "cc", "bcb", "bccb").

title: Table formatter with East Asian width
spec:
Write a Python function `format_table(headers: list[str], rows: list[list], align: str) -> str` that renders
a text table for a monospace terminal.
- Cell text = str(value), with None rendered as "". In every cell (and header) replace "|" with "\|" and
  "\n" with a single space, in that order.
- Display width of a string = sum over characters: 0 if unicodedata.combining(ch) != 0, else 2 if
  unicodedata.east_asian_width(ch) is "W" or "F", else 1.
- Column width = max display width over the header and all cells of that column (may be 0).
- align has exactly one character per column: 'l' (pad right), 'r' (pad left), 'c' (center: left padding =
  floor(extra / 2), right padding = the rest). Padding uses spaces.
- Output lines: header line, separator line, then one line per row, joined with "\n" (no trailing newline).
  A content line is "| " + " | ".join(padded cells) + " |". The separator line is
  "|" + "|".join("-" * (w + 2) for each column width w) + "|".
- Rows shorter than headers are padded with empty cells. Raise ValueError if a row is longer than headers, if
  len(align) != len(headers), or if align contains a character other than l, r, c.

title: Business-day arithmetic, strict dates
spec:
Write a Python function `add_business_days(start: str, n: int, holidays: list[str]) -> str`.
Dates are strings in the exact format YYYY-MM-DD (4-digit year, 2-digit month, 2-digit day, hyphens);
anything else (e.g. "20260930", "2026-9-30", "2026-02-30", " 2026-09-30") raises ValueError — this applies to
`start` and to every entry of `holidays`. A business day is Monday-Friday and not in holidays (holidays may
contain duplicates and weekend dates).
- n > 0: return the date reached after moving forward over exactly n business days, not counting `start`
  itself (whether or not start is a business day). n < 0: the same, moving backward over |n| business days.
- n == 0: return start if it is a business day, otherwise the next business day after it.
Return the result in YYYY-MM-DD format. |n| can be up to 100000 and holidays up to 10000 entries;
must run in under 1 second.

title: Sliding-window median (n=200k)
spec:
Write a Python function `sliding_median(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[float]` returning the median of every
contiguous window of size k (len(nums) - k + 1 results, left to right). For odd k the median is the middle
element; for even k it is (a + b) / 2 of the two middle elements. Every result is a Python float.
If k > len(nums) return []. If k <= 0 raise ValueError. Values may repeat and be negative.
Must handle len(nums) = 200_000 with k = 2_000 in under 2 seconds.

title: Strict canonical Roman parser
spec:
Write a Python function `parse_roman_strict(s: str) -> int` that accepts ONLY the canonical modern Roman
numeral for a value in 1..3999 (uppercase, standard subtractive pairs IV IX XL XC CD CM only, no more than
three consecutive identical symbols, largest-to-smallest order) and returns its value. Any other string
(empty, lowercase, "IIII", "IC", "VX", "MMMM", "IIX", "XIIII", "VV", "DCD", non-Roman characters, leading or
trailing spaces, ...) raises ValueError.

title: Spreadsheet evaluator (cycles, error precedence)
spec:
Write a Python function `evaluate_sheet(cells: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, object]` that evaluates a tiny
spreadsheet and returns a dict with a value for EVERY key of `cells`.
- Cell names: one uppercase letter A-Z followed by a row number 1-999 without leading zeros (e.g. "B12").
- Raw content: if it starts with "=", it is a formula. Otherwise, if it fully matches an optional sign followed
  by decimal digits (regex [+-]?[0-9]+, no surrounding spaces) it is that int; otherwise it is a text value
  (the raw string as is).
- Formula grammar (after the "="): int literals, cell references (uppercase only), binary + - * /, unary -,
  parentheses, and SUM(X1:Y2) where the argument is a rectangular range given by any two opposite corners.
  Spaces are allowed between tokens. / is integer division truncating toward zero. Anything else (including an
  empty formula, lowercase references, SUM without a range) is malformed.
- Values: an absent cell counts as 0. A text cell used as an operand gives "#VALUE!". SUM adds the int values
  in the range and skips text and absent cells (but errors in the range propagate).
- Errors are the strings "#ERROR!" (malformed formula), "#VALUE!", "#DIV/0!", "#CYCLE!". Evaluate operands
  left to right; the first error encountered becomes the result (for SUM, scan the range row by row top to
  bottom, left to right within a row). A malformed formula yields "#ERROR!" regardless of anything else.
- Cycles: consider the static dependency graph (a formula depends on every cell it names, including every
  cell inside its SUM ranges, whether or not it exists). Every well-formed formula cell that lies on a cycle
  (including a self-reference) evaluates to "#CYCLE!". Cells that merely depend on such cells get "#CYCLE!"
  through the normal first-error rule.
- Must handle dependency chains of 900 cells.

title: O(1) LFU cache class
spec:
Implement a Python class `LFUCache`:
- `__init__(self, capacity: int)` (capacity >= 0).
- `get(self, key)` returns the value or -1 if absent; a successful get increments the key's use count.
- `put(self, key, value)` inserts or updates. Updating an existing key changes its value and increments its
  use count. Inserting a NEW key when the cache is full first evicts the key with the smallest use count;
  among keys with that smallest count, evict the least recently used one (a get or put counts as a use).
  A newly inserted key has use count 1. With capacity 0, put does nothing.
Both operations must be O(1) average (200k operations in well under 2 seconds).
